chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan, from al-Husayn his brother, from his father Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Abu al-Hasan al-Madi (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about drinking al-fuqqa' (a type of beer/drink) which is made in the market and sold, and I do not know how it was made or when it was made. Is it permissible for me to drink it? He said: 'I do not like it.'

key_terms.أَبُو الْحَسَنِ الْمَاضِي: Abu al-Hasan al-Madi, referring to Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him), the sixth Imam.
key_terms.أَحْمَدَ بْنِ مُحَمَّدٍ: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, a prominent narrator in Shia hadith collections.
key_terms.الْفُقَّاع: Al-fuqqa', a type of beer or fermented drink made from barley or wheat, commonly consumed in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabia.
key_terms.عَلِيَّ بْنِ يَقْطِينَ: Ali ibn Yaqtin, a companion of the Imams known for narrating hadiths.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on drinking beer or fermented beverages sold in the market when their preparation method is unknown?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) expresses *karahat* (dislike/preference for caution) regarding 'al-fuqqa'' when its preparation method is unknown, reflecting the Shia principle of avoiding potential impurities (*najis*) or intoxicants (*khamr*) in commercial goods. This ruling highlights the importance of verifying the source and processing of consumables in Islamic jurisprudence, particularly when the distinction between mild fermentation and intoxication is unclear. The context of Chapter 55 further links this to the broader theme of purity, extending the caution from animal hides to ingestible substances.
